text: Albania's revised 2027 fiscal package drops a corporate‑tax increase and introduces lower VAT on basic foods, higher standard VAT, a new 30% top‑income tax rate and a lower turnover threshold for VAT registration, the government says. Opposition leaders, including Sali Berisha and Ervin Salianji, denounce the measures as harmful to businesses, while Prime Minister Edi Rama defended them on X as a fair redistribution of growth benefits.

sources.title: Albania’s 2027 Fiscal Package Sparks Backlash Over Higher Taxes and Investment Risks - Tirana Times
sources.articleText:
The American Chamber of Commerce warns of risks to foreign investment as the government’s 2027 fiscal package faces growing opposition from businesses, lawmakers and economists.
TIRANA, Albania , Oct. 29 – Albania’s government has unveiled a controversial 2027 fiscal package, proposing significant changes to value-added tax, dividend taxation, personal income taxes, and small-business obligations. Prime Minister Edi Rama has presented the measures on October 28 as an effort to redistribute the benefits of economic growth, but business organizations and opposition parties have strongly criticized the proposals, warning of higher prices, weaker competitiveness, and declining investment.
The package comes at a sensitive political moment. Albania is facing widespread student-led anti-government protests, growing public dissatisfaction over corruption and economic conditions, and increasingly confrontational relations between the government and opposition. Student-led demonstrations, fueled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs, and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana since mid-October and spread to other cities.
The proposed changes would reduce VAT on 54 basic food products from 20% to 6%, while increasing the standard VAT rate from 20% to 21%. VAT on hotel accommodation would rise from 6% to 10%, with an exception for agritourism businesses. The dividend tax would increase from 8% to 15%, while corporate income tax would remain unchanged at 15%.
In the initial draft of the package, which circulated before the formal Oct. 28 presentation, the government proposed raising the corporate income tax rate from 15% to 17%. That proposal was dropped. Several statements from business associations and opposition politicians made on Oct. 27 referenced the original draft and the 17% rate, a distinction worth noting when evaluating those reactions.
Another significant measure would lower the annual turnover threshold for mandatory VAT registration from 10 million lek to 5 million lek, bringing an estimated 17,500 additional businesses into the system. The measure is expected to affect small enterprises and independent professionals, including consultants, lawyers, engineers and other service providers.
The government also proposes changes to personal income taxation. The upper threshold for the 13% salary tax bracket would increase from 200,000 lek to 300,000 lek per month, benefiting approximately 32,000 taxpayers, according to Rama. A new 30% tax rate would apply to monthly salaries exceeding 700,000 lek. That rate was initially set at 32% in the preliminary draft but was revised downward during the Oct. 28 presentation.
Additionally, a new revenue control bureau at the Finance Ministry will also be established to check the income declarations of high earners and ensure that retailers are actually lowering the price for basic food products.
Other measures include restructuring the circulation tax on fuel and vehicles and introducing a separate circulation charge for foreign vehicles entering Albania.
According to the government, reducing VAT on essential foods could leave approximately 150 million euros annually in the hands of Albanian households. Finance Minister Petrit Malaj described the package as broadly revenue-neutral, designed to promote tax fairness, protect vulnerable households and strengthen revenue collection. Presenting the package at the Conference of Chairpersons, Malaj said the plan rests on three principles: income redistribution, greater tax fairness and improved tax system efficiency.
On Oct. 27, ahead of the formal presentation, Rama responded on social media platform X to early criticism. “Keep talking, keep talking about the new fiscal measures. Keep tossing your salad of hatred and ignorance with half-baked working documents, because tomorrow it will be the government’s turn to have its say with the approval of the first budget in history to exceed the 10 billion euro threshold and the most ambitious package for redistributing the benefits of economic growth,” Rama wrote.
However, the government’s calculations have raised questions about the actual distribution of the proposed benefits and costs. Although lower VAT on basic foods could provide relief to lower-income households, the reduction would not necessarily translate into equivalent retail price decreases. Much would depend on whether retailers pass the tax savings on to consumers and whether authorities can effectively monitor prices. Higher VAT on other goods and services could meanwhile increase household expenditures, potentially offsetting part of the expected savings.
Political opposition to the package has been strong, though some of the earliest statements were made in response to the initial draft that still included a 17% corporate tax.
Sali Berisha, leader of the Democratic Party and former prime minister, accused the government in an Oct. 27 video statement of preparing substantial tax increases without adequate consultation. He described the package as “an act of disloyalty” and warned that the measures would “lead to the bankruptcy of hundreds of thousands of businesses and the destruction of hundreds of thousands of jobs.” Berisha pledged that his party would reverse the changes if it returned to power, introduce a 10% flat tax, and raise the VAT registration threshold to 15 million lek.
Democratic Party Member of Parliament Ervin Salianji, a member of the party’s economic commission, was similarly direct. “Business is not the government’s ATM,” Salianji wrote in a public statement. “Entrepreneurs are not at fault for working and making a profit. Citizens should not have to pay for abuses of power.” He specifically objected to the VAT threshold reduction, warning that “the more corruption there is, the more taxes businesses, freelancers and the tourism sector face.”
